title: sync: WaitGroup (and wg.Go), Mutex/RWMutex, Once/OnceValue, atomic
summary: When goroutines share memory instead of passing it, package sync guards it: WaitGroup waits for them, Mutex and RWMutex serialise access, OnceValue runs initialisation exactly once, and sync/atomic handles lone counters and flags.

examples.title: wg.Go starts and counts goroutines; a Mutex guards the shared map

annotations.note: The mutex sits next to the data it guards, and both are unexported: callers go through add and can't forget the lock. The zero Mutex is unlocked and ready, so there is no constructor.

Lock, then defer Unlock on the next line, so an early return or a panic can't leave it locked. Go's Mutex isn't reentrant: calling add from inside add would block forever, where Java's synchronized would let the same thread in again.

wg.Go (Go 1.25) adds 1 before the goroutine starts and calls Done when the function returns. The older wg.Add(1); go func() { defer wg.Done() ... }() form is what go fix's waitgroupgo analyzer rewrites into this. Each iteration has its own line variable (Go 1.22), so no copy is needed.
Every goroutine's return happens before Wait returns, so their writes are visible here and reading the map without the lock is safe. Before Wait, it would be a data race.

examples.title: OnceValues for lazy initialisation, errors included

annotations.note: atomic.Int32 (Go 1.19) is the typed form: the value can only be reached through atomic methods, unlike a plain int32 handed to atomic.AddInt32 and read directly elsewhere.

OnceValues (Go 1.21) returns a function that runs f at most once. Callers that arrive while it runs wait for it, then everyone gets the same values. It replaces sync.Once plus package-level variables for the result and the error.
Each goroutine writes its own element of a pre-sized slice. Distinct elements are distinct memory locations, so this needs no lock and is race-free.

The error is cached too: three calls, one dial. If a failed attempt should be retried later, OnceValues is the wrong tool; keep the connection in a mutex-guarded field that stays nil until a dial succeeds.

examples.title: RWMutex for read-mostly data, atomics for counters

annotations.note: RWMutex admits many readers or one writer. It helps only when reads dominate: a waiting Lock blocks new RLock calls, so with frequent writes readers queue behind every writer anyway.
Several readers hold RLock at the same time, so c.hits++ on a plain int here would be a data race. RLock protects reading the map, not writing the counters; that's why the counters are atomics.
Writes take the exclusive lock. Concurrent writes to a Go map can crash the program with "fatal error: concurrent map writes", a fatal error rather than a panic, so recover can't catch it.
The 100 goroutines interleave differently on every run, yet the totals are fixed: 50 readers times two hits, 50 misses for "fr", and 2 + 50 entries.

use_cases: WaitGroup: wait for a batch of goroutines that report through shared memory or not at all; when they can fail, use errgroup (lesson 6)
Mutex: a map or struct that many request goroutines update, such as an in-memory cache, a session table or per-client rate-limit state
RWMutex: read-mostly data such as a routing table or a feature-flag set reloaded once a minute
OnceValue/OnceValues: lazy initialisation of templates, compiled regexps or a client, instead of init() or a hand-written nil check under a lock
atomic: counters, flags, and swapping in a new immutable config snapshot with atomic.Pointer[T]
strengths: Zero values are ready to use: var mu sync.Mutex and var wg sync.WaitGroup need no constructor, unlike Java's new ReentrantLock()
go vet catches copied locks (copylocks) and wg.Add called inside the new goroutine (waitgroup); javac and C++ compilers check neither
OnceValue is lazy, thread-safe initialisation in one line, without Java's double-checked locking and its volatile subtleties
Atomics are sequentially consistent, the semantics of C++'s default std::atomic and Java's volatile, so there are no memory orderings to choose
weaknesses: Nothing ties a mutex to the data it guards. Unlike Rust's Mutex<T>, the compiler can't tell you a field was read without the lock; only the race detector can, at run time
No reentrancy: a goroutine that locks a mutex it already holds blocks forever
No lock timeouts like Java's tryLock(timeout, unit); TryLock exists, but its own docs call correct uses rare

pitfalls.title: Copying a value that contains a lock
pitfalls.detail: A value receiver or a struct passed by value copies the mutex, and each copy locks independently, which protects nothing. Use pointer receivers; go vet's copylocks check reports the copy.
pitfalls.bad: func (c cache) get(k string) string { c.mu.RLock(); defer c.mu.RUnlock(); return c.data[k] }
pitfalls.good: func (c *cache) get(k string) string { c.mu.RLock(); defer c.mu.RUnlock(); return c.data[k] }

pitfalls.title: Calling wg.Add inside the goroutine
pitfalls.detail: Wait may run before the goroutine has called Add and return early. Call Add before the go statement, or let wg.Go do both; go vet's waitgroup analyzer (Go 1.25) reports the misplaced Add.
pitfalls.bad: go func() { wg.Add(1); defer wg.Done(); work() }()

pitfalls.title: Locking the same mutex twice in one call chain
pitfalls.detail: A locked method that calls another locked method on the same value blocks forever. Split it into a public method that locks and an unexported helper that assumes the lock is held.
pitfalls.bad: func (s *Store) Move(a, b string) { s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock(); s.Delete(a); s.Put(b) } // Delete and Put lock s.mu too
pitfalls.good: func (s *Store) Move(a, b string) { s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock(); s.deleteLocked(a); s.putLocked(b) }

pitfalls.title: Holding a lock across I/O
pitfalls.detail: An HTTP call or a database query under a mutex serialises every caller behind the slowest request. Copy what you need, unlock, then do the I/O.

quiz.q: A method holds mu.RLock() and increments a plain int field. Is that safe?
options: No: several readers can hold RLock at once, so the increment races
quiz.why: RLock is shared. Writes need Lock, or the counter needs to be an atomic.

quiz.q: The function passed to sync.OnceValues returned an error on its first call. What do later calls return?
options: The same error, without calling the function
quiz.why: OnceValues runs the function once and caches both results, the error included.

quiz.q: A method holding s.mu.Lock() calls another method of s that also calls s.mu.Lock(). What happens?
options: It works, the lock is reentrant
quiz.why: Go's Mutex has no owner and no reentrancy, so the second Lock waits for an Unlock that never comes.

quiz.q: Many goroutines increment one shared counter. What is the simplest correct choice?
quiz.why: A lone counter is what atomics are for. A plain int races, and sync.Map is a map for specific access patterns, not a counter.

further_reading.title: Go 1.25 release notes: WaitGroup.Go and the waitgroup vet check

body:
## Concept

Lesson 1 passed data between goroutines through channels. The alternative is to share
memory and guard it. Package `sync` and `sync/atomic` provide the tools:

- **`WaitGroup`**: wait until a set of goroutines has finished. `wg.Go(f)` (Go 1.25)
  starts `f` in a goroutine and counts it; `wg.Wait()` blocks until all have returned.
- **`Mutex`**: one goroutine at a time in the critical section. **`RWMutex`**: many
  readers or one writer.
- **`Once`**, **`OnceFunc`**, **`OnceValue`**, **`OnceValues`** (the last three since
  Go 1.21): run something exactly once, on first use, safely from any goroutine.
- **`sync/atomic`**: typed atomics such as `atomic.Int64`, `atomic.Bool` and
  `atomic.Pointer[T]` (Go 1.19) for single values.

The types (`WaitGroup`, `Mutex`, `RWMutex`, `Once`, the atomics) are ready to use as zero
values and must not be copied after first use.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: `Mutex` ≈ `ReentrantLock` without the reentrancy, and there is no
  `synchronized` keyword, so a lock is always an explicit field. `WaitGroup` ≈
  `CountDownLatch` with a counter you can increase. `OnceValue` replaces lazy holders
  and double-checked locking. `atomic.Int64` ≈ `AtomicLong`.
- **C/C++**: `Mutex` ≈ `std::mutex`, with `defer mu.Unlock()` in place of
  `std::lock_guard`. Go atomics are always sequentially consistent, like
  `std::atomic` with the default `memory_order_seq_cst`; there is no relaxed mode.
- **Python**: `threading.Lock` maps directly. The difference: goroutines run in parallel
  on all cores, with no GIL serialising them, so a missing lock corrupts data quickly.
- **JS**: one event loop never needs locks between callbacks. Go's goroutines are
  preemptively scheduled across threads, so any shared write needs one of these tools.

## How it works

The guarantees come from the Go memory model, which defines "synchronizes before":
an `Unlock` synchronizes before the next `Lock`, the return of a `wg.Go` function before
the `Wait` it releases, and the return of a `Once` function before any `once.Do` call
returns. Without such an edge, a write in one goroutine and a read in another are a
**data race**: the read may see the old value or the new one, and for multiword values
such as strings, slices and interfaces a torn mix that can corrupt memory. Lesson 6
shows how the race detector finds them.

Typed atomics are the safer form. `var n int64` plus `atomic.AddInt64(&n, 1)` compiles
fine next to a plain `n++` somewhere else; `var n atomic.Int64` has no plain access at
all. In the Go 1.27 toolchain, `go fix`'s `atomictypes` analyzer rewrites the old form
into the new one.

## Design notes

Channels or mutexes? Use a channel when ownership moves, such as handing a job to a
worker or passing a result back. Use a mutex when several goroutines need short access
to the same structure, like a cache or a counter table. "Share memory by communicating"
is the default, not a ban: a mutex around a map is simpler than a goroutine that owns
the map and serves requests over channels.

Keep critical sections small and free of I/O. Put the mutex in the struct it protects,
unexported, with methods that lock, so callers can't forget. Prefer `Mutex` over
`RWMutex` until reads clearly dominate.

`sync.Map` is not a general replacement for a map plus a mutex. Its docs say most code
should use a plain map, and name the two cases it is optimized for: keys written once
and read many times, and goroutines working on disjoint key sets. Otherwise a plain map
with a mutex keeps type safety and lets you maintain other invariants under the same
lock.
